items.title: Markets React to Geopolitical Tensions and Fed Outlook.
items.excerpt: Bob Iaccino of Path Trading Partners recaps the morning's market action as U.S. equities open lower, led by a drop in Nasdaq futures. He covers rising diesel prices tied to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and breaks down the latest global economic data, including UK jobs and Eurozone sentiment. Domestically, U.S. housing starts are in focus alongside declining precious metals and climbing U.S. Treasury yields. Iaccino also examines the CME FedWatch Tool's shifting probabilities for a September rate hike ahead of critical FOMC minutes, wrapping up with a look at upcoming major retail earnings from Target, Lowe's, and TJX.

items.title: Luxury stocks are on sale. But is anything actually cheap?
items.excerpt: Key takeaways China is not disappearing as a luxury market, but consumers are becoming more selective about where they spend. Years of price increases have tested the limits of what aspirational customers are willing to pay. European luxury shares have come under pressure, reflecting weaker growth, more cautious consumers and high expectations built up over previous years. Lower share prices do not automatically create opportunities, but they are making the investment question more interesting. items.title: Copper versus gold: what an old macro signal is telling us now
items.excerpt: Key Points: Copper-to-gold ratio remains historically low : Around 3.24, still signaling gold s strength, though copper has recently recovered slightly. Macro signal is less clear : Copper reflects industrial demand, but electrification, AI buildout, supply constraints, and geopolitics now play a larger role; gold is supported by central bank buying and diversification. Copper is still an industrial meta l: Higher prices can trigger substitution, efficiency gains, and demand destruction. Gold faces fewer constraints : Driven by investment and central banks, it is less exposed to demand destruction and may outperform in a risk-hedging environment. items.title: Why higher yields are changing the investment playbook
items.excerpt: Key takeaways: Capital is getting more expensive: governments, AI, defence and infrastructure are all competing for funding. Higher yields may mean something different: if fiscal risk is driving yields, the dollar may not strengthen and gold may stay supported. Portfolio leadership could shift: investors may increasingly favour cash generation, balance-sheet strength, income and diversification over leverage and long-duration bets. Capital may be becoming the market's next scarce resource For much of the post-global-financial-crisis era, investors operated under an implicit assumption: capital was abundant. Home Depot and Klarna test appetite for larger purchases when confidence and borrowing costs still matter. Carlsberg and Est e Lauder show whether small indulgences remain resilient across different markets. US retail sales fell 0.6% in July, while consumer sentiment weakened again in early August. items.excerpt: Bob Iaccino of Path Trading Partners breaks down price action in British Pound futures as the September contract reached a three-month high before settling higher for the session. items.title: The FX Trader: Long US yields keep the dollar and carry trades alive.
items.excerpt: USD edges higher after in-line CPI The latest US CPI fails to knock down long-end yields or the US dollar. Yesterday s July US CPI report landed almost precisely on expectations, with headline CPI rising 0.1% month-on-month and core CPI up 0.2%. The kneejerk reaction was straightforward enough: Treasury yields fell across the curve and the US dollar weakened. But the more interesting development came later, as only the front end of the Treasury curve retained much of the move. The result was a bull steepening of the US yield curve, with longer-dated yields giving back much of their initial decline. That distinction matters for the US dollar. A modest repricing of the next Fed move can pull the two-year yield lower, but the dollar may prove considerably harder to dislodge if the US…

items.title: Swiss Franc futures hit 2-week low ahead of inflation data.
items.excerpt: Bob Iaccino of Path Trading Partners outlines recent price action in Swiss Franc futures, noting the contract's drop to its lowest level since July 29. With the franc falling for a third consecutive session, Iaccino looks ahead to tomorrow's Swiss producer and import prices, explaining how another soft reading could align with July's tame inflation report. He highlights the ongoing policy divergence between the Swiss National Bank, which holds its rate at 0%, and the U.S. Federal Reserve, observing that central bank decisions will continue to drive currency market dynamics.

He breaks down the reaction across asset classes, noting lower yields and broad gains in precious and base metals. Iaccino also highlights ongoing geopolitical risks in the Middle East concerning the U.S. and Iran, which continue to loom over energy markets despite crude oil's intraday dip. Finally, he outlines what traders should watch next, including the upcoming PPI inflation data, global economic reports, and key mega-cap corporate earnings.

items.title: Euro futures held near 7-week highs ahead of key CPI and PPI data.
items.excerpt: Dan Deming from KKM Financial analyzes FX markets as Euro futures trade slightly lower but hold near their recent seven-week highs. Market action remains quiet and range-bound across major currency pairs as traders await crucial Wednesday CPI and Thursday PPI inflation data. Deming also notes tight trading ranges in metals, slight selling pressure in equities, and higher prices on the back end of the Treasury curve, emphasizing that upcoming inflation numbers and their interpretation by the Fed will be the primary catalyst for the week.
